paragraph.text: it's the reductio ad Hitlerum: trying to discredit an idea by associating it with a hated figure. It's a poorly built association, meant to discredit, and it proves nothing: Hitler also painted, and that doesn't make artists bad people; he didn't smoke, and that doesn't make cigarettes good. And the historical question is more complicated than the slogan: he adopted a meat-free diet inconsistently, from the 1930s and mostly for health reasons, there are accounts of him eating meat at various times before the war, and he certainly wasn't vegan, since he ate eggs and dairy. The Nazi regime, in fact, pressured German vegetarian associations, and the main one dissolved in 1935.

Some very bad people did ordinary things, like drinking water, painting pictures or liking dogs. That doesn't make those things bad. What matters is whether an idea is right, not who else thought something similar. Hurting animals without needing to doesn't become right just because a bad person also didn't eat meat.

Even if Hitler had been vegetarian, that would say nothing about veganism. He also painted, and you don't think artists are bad people because of it. It's the so-called reductio ad Hitlerum: associating an idea with a hated figure to avoid discussing it. And the history is more complicated: he gave up meat inconsistently, mostly for health reasons, there are accounts of him eating meat at various times, and he certainly wasn't vegan, since he ate eggs and dairy. Leaving Hitler out of it, what matters is what happens to the animals: is it fair to make them suffer and die when we don't need to?

text.bold: 3. It proves nothing, because it proves too much.

paragraph.text: Hitler also painted: he twice tried to get into the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna (1907 and 1908) and, for a few years, lived by selling watercolors and paintings of the city's buildings. No one concludes from this that painting is bad or that artists are bad people. Picking, from a hated person's many habits, precisely the one you want to discredit says nothing about that habit.

text.bold: 4. The historical question is more complicated than the slogan.

paragraph.text: Accounts of Hitler's diet before the Second World War are inconsistent, and several mention meat, such as sausages and liver dumplings. He began avoiding meat inconsistently from the 1930s, mostly because of digestive and health problems; in the last years of the war, accounts point to a meat-free diet, and the image of an austere vegetarian leader was also cultivated by propaganda. Historians still debate whether "vegetarian" accurately describes his diet over his lifetime.

Even in his meat-free periods, Hitler ate eggs and dairy, such as cottage cheese, and wore leather. The word "vegan" was only coined in 1944, when the Vegan Society was founded in the UK. The argument talks about a "vegetarian" and tries to conclude something about vegans.

text.bold: 6. The regime was no friend of organized vegetarianism.

paragraph.text: Germany's main vegetarian association, the Deutscher Vegetarierbund, had its magazine stopped in 1933 and dissolved in February 1935 under pressure from the regime, which accused vegetarian groups of promoting pacifism; several groups of the life-reform movement were banned or forced to dissolve. Accessible sources on the details are limited, but the overall picture is not that of a vegetarian regime.

text.bold: 7. The Nazi regime used animals in experiments.

paragraph.text: Its supposed concern for animals was selective and instrumental.

text.bold: 8. Concern for animals doesn't require contempt for humans.

paragraph.text: A small neuroimaging study even suggested the opposite, that vegans and vegetarians react more strongly to human suffering; it's modest evidence, but nothing links concern for animals to contempt for people (L21).

text.bold: 9. The Nazi association has been used before, and the answer is the same.

paragraph.text: In a 1977 critique of animal protection, the Marxist philosopher Howard Parsons remarked, in parentheses, that some Nazis were fond of animals. The political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane replies that a moral claim should be judged on its merits, not by who makes it: even if some animal advocates were Nazis, that wouldn't invalidate what they say, just as the social background of those who called for the end of slavery didn't make abolition wrong (Cochrane, 2010, pp. 102–104). It's the genetic fallacy: judging an idea by its origin.

It's true that concern for animals doesn't make anyone virtuous, and that violent regimes have used animal protection rhetoric selectively. No one should assume that someone who cares for animals is automatically good.
But that says nothing about whether it's right to eat animals. The question needs to be answered with arguments, not associations.
